title: AI Cracks 10 Tough Math Problems, But the Riemann Hypothesis Still Stands
summary:
Artificial intelligence is making waves in the world of mathematics. On August 1, OpenAI announced that its new model, Astra, resolved or made progress on 10 long-standing mathematical problems, including Connes's rigidity conjecture and Ehrhart's volume conjecture. Meanwhile, Anthropic revealed that an unreleased version of Claude made strides on the Riemann hypothesis using the Riemann zeta function.

The Riemann hypothesis, proposed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, is considered the most significant open problem in math. It's one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, with a $1 million reward. The hypothesis states that every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function has real part 1/2. Solving it would unlock an avalanche of progress in number theory and analysis.

Anthropic cautioned that Claude's techniques likely won't lead to a proof, but the progress showcases AI's growing mathematical capabilities. Mathematicians are both excited and skeptical, according to The Verge. In June, researchers proposed the Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics, calling for ethical guardrails to uphold research integrity.

Other famous unsolved problems include the Collatz conjecture and Goldbach's conjecture. The Collatz conjecture involves a simple function: if a number is even, halve it; if odd, triple it and add 1. The conjecture states you always reach 1, but no proof exists. Goldbach's conjecture, from 1742, posits that every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes.

As AI pushes the boundaries, the question remains: will a human or a machine solve these puzzles first? For now, you can take a crack at them—maybe you'll make history.
why_it_matters: If AI becomes a serious tool for proving or guiding mathematics, it could reshape how human mathematicians work, who gets credit, and how results are verified. It also raises ethical questions about transparency, collaboration, and access to powerful research tools.

background_read: OpenAI (the artificial-intelligence company behind ChatGPT) and Anthropic (a rival AI lab known for the Claude chatbot) are both racing to show that their systems can help with advanced mathematics, not just writing or coding.

Bernhard Riemann (a 19th-century German mathematician) proposed the Riemann hypothesis in 1859, and it has resisted proof ever since, despite being one of the most famous unsolved problems in the field.
It is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, a list of major open problems that each carry a $1 million reward, and it remains unproved.
Other open problems include the Collatz conjecture, which is easy to state but has never been solved, and Goldbach's conjecture, which concerns sums of prime numbers.

The Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics is a recent proposal by researchers to set ethical guardrails as AI becomes a bigger part of mathematical work, not just a black-box answer machine.

perspectives.description: AI can explore huge search spaces and spot patterns that humans might miss, potentially speeding up work on stubborn problems. Even partial progress on conjectures can inspire new approaches and make difficult math more accessible.
Some mathematicians worry that AI results may be overhyped or unverified. Without rigorous proofs, impressive-sounding progress can mislead the public and undermine trust in mathematical research.

This is part of a longer pattern of computation in mathematics, from calculator-assisted calculations to computer-assisted proofs. The real question is how human judgment and machine pattern-finding should share the proof process.

Ethical guardrails like those proposed in the Leiden Declaration could shape norms for AI-assisted math. Peer review, funding, and education may need to adapt if AI systems become regular research partners.
